blocks.c: Somewhere out there is a site you already read on. A web-novel archive, a translation group's house, a serial that updates on Tuesdays. The usual arrangement is that you go to it — through a browser, past the pop-ups, into whatever that site believes a reading experience is. This chapter is about the reverse arrangement.

Open Add series on the home screen and choose Add by link. Paste the address of a series page — the page that lists its chapters — and the app fetches that list, shows you exactly what it found, and waits for you to confirm before anything joins the shelf. What arrives is that series inside this reader: your typography, your themes, your saved place, laid over their chapters. Nothing is copied to any server along the way; the arrangement is between your device and theirs.

Do that twice for one site and you will want the site itself within reach. That is what sources are for. On the sources screen you can save it — a name, an address, nothing more — and it appears on your home screen as a shelf of its own. Saved sources are bookmarks with superpowers: tap one and you can browse the site's catalogue from inside the app, covers and all, and add any series you find from right where you stand. Anything already on your shelf is marked as such while you browse, so you will not shelve the same book twice by accident. The shelf holds twenty-four sources, and when it is full the app says so plainly rather than quietly discarding an old friend.

Now the honest part. Browsing someone else's site from inside an app takes a small helper — a content gateway that fetches pages and reads chapter lists on your behalf. It is optional equipment, and some installations run without it. When it is off, the app tells you so, in plain words, exactly where the browsing would have been. Your saved sources still work as ordinary links that open the site itself; nothing spins forever, and nothing pretends.
An app should tell you what it cannot do in the same calm voice it uses for what it can. Anything else is theater.

Sources are also, frankly, a bet on your taste. The catalogue that ships with this app is deliberately small — one tutorial and six old classics — because the interesting shelf is the one you assemble yourself. The app brings the reader. You bring the library.
Next: what happens to all of these books once you are actually reading them. The long game.
